hints: Look for carbon atoms with four single bonds to four different groups, focus on the amino acid alpha carbons in the centre and right of the molecule.
walkthrough:
Recall what makes a carbon chiral**
Picture yourself sitting with the structure. A chiral carbon must have four different groups attached and no plane of symmetry. Quickly ignore $\text{CH}_{2}$, $\text{CH}_{3}$, $\text{C=O}$ and benzene carbons, they cannot be chiral.

Spot the two amino acid alpha carbons**
In the centre you see $\text{NH-CH(CH}_{2}\text{CO}_{2}\text{H)-C=O}$. That $\text{CH}$ is joined to $\text{H}$, $\text{NH}$, $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ and $\text{C=O}$, four different groups. On the right you see $\text{NH-CH(CH}_{2}\text{Ph)-CO}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$. That $\text{CH}$ is joined to $\text{H}$, $\text{NH}$, $\text{CH}_{2}\text{Ph}$ and $\text{CO}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, also four different groups. Those are the two to circle.

Final answer: Circle the two alpha carbons: the $\text{CH}$ bearing $\text{NH}$ and $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ in the middle, and the $\text{CH}$ bearing $\text{NH}$ and $\text{CH}_{2}\text{Ph}$ on the right.

hints: Compare Advantame with J + K + L and notice an amide $\text{CONH}$ has become $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ + $\text{NH}_{2}$ and an ester $\text{CO}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ has become $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$.
walkthrough:
Read the bond changes**
Look at the middle amide $\text{CO-NH}$ in Advantame. In products it is split into $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ in J and $\text{H}_{2}\text{N}$ in K. On the right the methyl ester $\text{CO}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ becomes $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ in K. Both are hydrolysis reactions that need water added across the bond.

Choose the classic hydrolysis conditions**
For A Level, amides and esters are hydrolysed by heating with dilute aqueous acid. So suggest $\text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)}$ plus heat, for example warm dilute hydrochloric acid.
Final answer: Dilute aqueous $\text{H}^{+}$, e.g. dilute $\text{HCl(aq)}$ or $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}\text{(aq)}$, with heat.

hints: Think of the name given when water splits an amide or ester into acid plus amine or alcohol.
walkthrough:
Name the water splitting process**
You are adding $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ across $\text{C=O}$ bonds to break them. The general name for cleavage by water is hydrolysis, here acid hydrolysis of an amide and an ester.
Final answer: Hydrolysis.

hints: Balance atoms between Advantame plus water and J + K, and see which small alcohol must come from the $\text{OCH}_{3}$ group.
walkthrough:
Find the missing fragment**
J accounts for the left side ending in $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$, K accounts for phenylalanine ending in $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$. The only atoms of Advantame not yet accounted for are the $\text{OCH}_{3}$ of the methyl ester. Hydrolysis of $\text{CO}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ with water gives $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ + $\text{CH}_{3}\text{OH}$. So L is methanol, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{OH}$.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{OH}$, methanol.

hints: Look at J on the left, it contains a benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ and $\text{OR}$ groups directly attached, recall how that ring reacts with bromine water.
walkthrough:
Recognise the phenol group**
J has $\text{HO}$ directly on the benzene ring, so it is a phenol. The $\text{OH}$ strongly activates the ring to electrophilic substitution.

Recall the bromine water result**
Phenols react instantly with aqueous $\text{Br}_{2}$ even without a catalyst to give a white precipitate of polybromo product, and the orange bromine colour disappears. With excess bromine you still see the white solid.
Final answer: White precipitate forms, bromine water is decolourised.

hints: List the acidic groups in J that react with NaOH, remembering the RO ether group is stated to be unreactive.
Count how many moles of NaOH are needed for two $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ groups plus one phenolic $\text{OH}$, then balance water formed.
walkthrough:
Count the acidic protons**
Sit with J: it has two carboxylic acid groups, $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$, each reacts with one $\text{NaOH}$. It has one phenol $\text{Ar-OH}$, which also reacts with one $\text{NaOH}$. The ether $\text{RO}$ and the secondary amine $\text{NH}$ do not consume $\text{NaOH}$ under these conditions. Total is 3 moles $\text{NaOH}$ per mole J.

Write the balanced molecular equation**
Each neutralisation makes one $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ and replaces $\text{H}$ by $\text{Na}$:
$$\text{C}_{14}\text{H}_{19}\text{O}_{6}\text{N} + 3\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_{14}\text{H}_{16}\text{O}_{6}\text{NNa}_{3} + 3\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$
Check: remove 3 acidic $\text{H}$ from J, add 3 $\text{Na}$, and form 3 $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. That balances.

hints: Check whether K has a phenol $\text{OH}$, an alkene, or just an ordinary phenyl ring attached via $\text{CH}_{2}$.
walkthrough:
See why K is different from J**
K is phenylalanine, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH(NH}_{2}\text{)CO}_{2}\text{H}$. The benzene ring has no $\text{OH}$ directly attached, it is not a phenol and not an alkene. Ordinary benzene does not react with aqueous bromine without a halogen carrier. So the orange bromine colour stays and no white solid appears.
Final answer: No change, solution remains orange, no precipitate.

hints: Identify the two functional groups in the amino acid K that can join together with loss of water.
Join $\text{NH}_{2}$ of one monomer to $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ of the next to make $\text{CONH}$, and repeat this to show two linked residues.
walkthrough:
Spot the condensation pair**
Each K has $\text{H}_{2}\text{N-}$ at one end and $-\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ at the other. The amine of one attacks the carboxylic acid of the next, losing $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ to form an amide link, $\text{-CO-NH-}$.

Draw two repeat units clearly**
Draw $\text{-NH-CH(CH}_{2}\text{Ph)-C(=O)-NH-CH(CH}_{2}\text{Ph)-C(=O)-}$ with the $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{N-H}$ fully displayed between the alpha carbons. Keep the side chain $\text{CH}_{2}\text{Ph}$ on each alpha carbon. Showing two amide linked residues earns both marks, one for the correct amide display and one for two repeats.

Final answer: Polyamide: $\text{-[NH-CH(CH}_{2}\text{Ph)-CO]-}_{n}$ shown as two units with full $\text{-C(=O)-NH-}$ linkage displayed, e.g. $\text{H-[N(H)-CH(CH}_{2}\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{)-C(=O)]}_{2}\text{-OH}$ with correct connectivity.

hints: Split K into the phenyl part and the side chain $\text{CH}_{2}$, $\text{CH}$ and $\text{C=O}$, then use symmetry of a monosubstituted benzene.
walkthrough:
Count unique carbons**
Label K: $\text{C=O}$ is 1, $\text{CH}$ is 1, $\text{CH}_{2}$ is 1. For $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}$, the ipso carbon attached to $\text{CH}_{2}$ is unique, the two ortho carbons are equivalent to each other, the two meta carbons are equivalent to each other, and the para carbon is unique. That is 4 ring environments. Total $3 + 4 = 7$ peaks.
Final answer: Seven different carbon environments.

hints: Recall from the Data Booklet the typical ranges for carbons in a benzene ring compared with carbons in a carboxylic acid $\text{C=O}$.
walkthrough:
Match shift to environment**
A shift around $\delta = 130$ is classic for $\text{C}$ in an aromatic ring, so circle any carbon in the $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}$ ring and label it x. A shift around $\delta = 170$ is classic for a carboxylic acid $\text{C=O}$, so circle the $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ carbon and label it y.
Final answer: x: any aryl carbon on the phenyl ring ($\delta$ 130); y: the carboxylic acid $\text{C=O}$ carbon ($\delta$ 170).
